Furtive

/FUR-tiv/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Furtive means done secretly or stealthily, in a way that suggests hidden or guilty intent.

He slid the report into his bag with a furtive glance toward the supervisor's office.

Worked Example

Halfway through the exam, the proctor noticed a student's odd rhythm: write, pause, drop the left hand below the desk, glance sideways, write again. Each movement was small and quick, timed for the moments the proctor turned toward the window. When she finally circled behind him, she found a strip of formulas taped inside his sleeve. It was the furtiveness of the gestures — not the gestures themselves — that had given him away.

The quick, concealed movements timed to escape the proctor's eye suggest hidden, guilty intent — that sneaky manner is exactly what furtive describes.

How Furtive Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

stealthy

stealthy: quiet and careful to avoid notice

sneaky

sneaky: acting slyly in secret

Antonyms

open

open: done in plain view

forthright

forthright: direct and honest in manner

How Strong Is It? — discreet → furtive → clandestine

discreet vs. furtive

discreet vs. furtive: Discreet is weaker than furtive: a discreet person keeps things quiet out of tact, with nothing to hide, while a furtive one moves as if caught halfway through a guilty act.

clandestine vs. furtive

clandestine vs. furtive: Clandestine is stronger than furtive — clandestine describes whole operations kept deliberately hidden, while furtive describes the darting, guilty manner of a single glance or gesture.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of furtive.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — furt

Root — furt: theft (Latin furtum, from fur, thief)

Suffix — -ive

Suffix — -ive: (fused inside Latin furtivus — not added in English)

Put it together

Put it together: Furtive is this unit's clearest false friend. It comes whole from Latin furtivus, 'stolen; thief-like,' built on furtum ('theft') from fur ('thief'). The '-ive' you see was already fused inside the Latin adjective — it was never added to an English or Latin base the way corroborate builds corroborative or instruct builds instructive. And the root fur left no common English family to check against (its likeliest descendant, ferret, is a fun rarity, not a pattern). So treat furtive as a single sealed unit: a furtive movement is 'thief-like' — done the way a thief moves.

Use the root in a new word: ferret

Use the root in a new word: ferret: A fun aside: ferret likely descends from Latin furittus, 'little thief' — the same fur ('thief') behind furtive, which is why ferreting something out means slyly digging up what was hidden.
